strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: any-reference video generation with three concrete failure modes (identity inconsistency, cross-subject entanglement, copy-paste artifacts) that are well connected to the proposed components.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: comparison against 12 baselines including 4 proprietary systems (Hailuo, Pika 2.1, Vidu 2.0, Kling 1.6) and 8 open-source methods, in both single-ID and multi-subject settings, with detailed generation protocols in the appendix.

Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3–4) covering the training paradigm, region-aware masking, cross-pair data strategy, and subject disentanglement, plus qualitative ablations (Figures 7–8) that convincingly illustrate failure modes of vanilla masking and token-wise concatenation.

The four-stage data curation pipeline is described in substantial detail (appendix B), including concrete filtering, segmentation, IoU-based conflict removal, and cross-pair augmentation steps that plausibly address copy-paste artifacts.
Includes a pairwise user study with 30 participants and a dedicated failure-case analysis (Figure 14, Appendix E.2/F), which adds credibility beyond cherry-picked qualitative results.
The region-aware masking + channel concatenation design preserves the I2V paradigm of the pretrained backbone, a sensible and practical design choice with quantitative support (Table 3).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is largely a careful combination of known conditioning strategies (channel concatenation as in VACE/SkyReels-A2, token-wise injection as in Phantom, region/semantic injection reminiscent of regional prompting and layout-guided methods like MS-Diffusion). The conceptual advance over these closely related works is incremental and the paper's differentiation is more empirical than methodological.

The core Subject Disentanglement mechanism (Eq. 6) is technically underspecified and possibly ill-defined: injecting text value embeddings vi ∈ R^D into a latent z0 ∈ R^(1×C×H×W) via Hadamard product 'with broadcasting' is dimensionally unclear, the weight α and the choice of layer(s)/timesteps are never specified, and how word labels are parsed and matched to subject regions K is not explained. This undermines confidence in the claimed contribution.

Contradictory claims about architecture: the abstract and contributions state 'without requiring any architectural changes' / 'minimal architectural modifications,' yet channel concatenation of (2C+Cm) input channels necessarily modifies the first-layer input dimension of the backbone; this inconsistency should be clarified.

Critical training details are missing: dataset scale (number of videos/pairs after curation), total GPU-hours, training duration, image-to-video training recipe, and inference settings are not reported, which harms reproducibility. The GitHub and project-page links are empty in the submitted version.

The evaluation benchmark is self-constructed (only 120 reference-text pairs), and some proposed metrics are questionable: Bg-Sim compares generated-video backgrounds against a 'ground-truth background' reconstructed by an inpainting model, which is ambiguous for a generation task with no ground-truth video; the composite Total Score equally weights metrics of very different reliability and no significance analysis or variance is reported.

Small gaps between the full model and ablations (e.g., 0.627 vs 0.580 Total Score) on a 60-case multi-subject benchmark may not be statistically significant; several ablations are run only 'on a small-scale dataset,' limiting their strength.

Evaluation is tied to a single backbone (Wan2.1); no evidence is provided that the approach generalizes across other video diffusion backbones, and comparisons across baselines involve differing resolutions/frame rates, complicating fairness.

Carelessness in the manuscript: duplicated references ([2]/[3], [16]/[17], [41]/[42]), a typo in 'mechansim,' dangling reference '(see 14),' and empty release links suggest the paper was not fully polished.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and timely task (any-reference/multi-subject video generation) and is generally well organized and easy to follow.

A comprehensive comparison against 12 open-source and proprietary baselines is reported, together with a user study and ablations of the main components (masking mechanism, concatenation strategy, subject disentanglement, data pipeline).
The four-stage data curation pipeline is described in reasonable detail in the appendix, and failure cases are honestly visualized.
The proposed approach requires no architectural changes to the pre-trained backbone, which is attractive from a practical standpoint.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core design (composing references on a canvas, VAE-encoding the composite, concatenating latents along the channel dimension with masks) is very close to existing work, particularly SkyReels-A2 [12] and VACE [21], which the authors acknowledge. The 'subject disentanglement' mechanism (Eq. 6) is a simple masked addition of text value embeddings and feels more like an engineering trick than a substantive methodological contribution; the injection procedure (which layer, which attention values, how α is chosen, how dimensions D vs. C are reconciled) is under-specified.

Questionable evaluation design. The benchmark is self-constructed (120 pairs) with limited curation detail. Several metrics are ill-defined for this task: Bg-Sim compares generated backgrounds against a 'ground-truth background' although the task is open-ended generation and there is no GT video; Subj-Sim relies on GroundingDINO+SAM2+DINO pipelines whose failure modes are not analyzed. Averaging heterogeneous metrics into a 'Total Score' is arbitrary. Baselines are run at different resolutions, durations, and frame rates, which confounds the comparison.

Insufficient training and reproducibility details. The dataset size, backbone scale, number of GPUs/steps, and Stage 4 image generation model (which is unnamed and likely proprietary) are not reported. The GitHub and Project Page links in the abstract are empty. The ablations are performed 'on a small-scale dataset with equal training steps,' so it is unclear whether conclusions transfer to the full-scale model.

Missing ablations and analyses: no analysis of sensitivity to the number of references (acknowledged as a limitation), no comparison of the subject disentanglement injection strength α, no statistical significance or confidence intervals for the quantitative results, and the user study (30 participants, 60 questions) lacks detail on demographic control and analysis methodology.

Notation-heavy presentation of trivial operations: Eqs. (1), (2), (5) merely formalize pasting images on a canvas and binary masking, while the actually non-trivial components (e.g., how word labels are parsed from captions, how subject regions are matched to text at inference time) are described only briefly.

Sloppy writing and bibliography: duplicated references ([2]/[3], [16]/[17], [41]/[42]), incorrect entries ([43], [44]), typos ('mechansim', 'Regional-aware Mask'), and empty links suggest the manuscript was not carefully prepared.

Ethical considerations are not addressed. The system is explicitly built to preserve and transfer human identities from single face images into controllable videos, and the data pipeline scrapes and processes faces from web videos. There is no discussion of consent, deepfake misuse potential, or safeguards—this is a significant omission for a paper of this nature.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and timely problem (any-reference/multi-subject video generation) and presents a unified, complete system built on a strong backbone (Wan2.1) that supports arbitrary combinations of subjects without architectural changes to the pre-trained model.

Evaluation is comparatively thorough for this area: a 120-case benchmark spanning single-ID and multi-subject settings, comparisons against 8 open-source and 4 proprietary models, a user study with 30 participants, and ablations of each of the three proposed components (Tables 3-4), with both quantitative and qualitative evidence.

The four-stage data curation pipeline is described in unusual detail (Appendix B), including concrete filtering rules, thresholds, and augmentation strategies for mitigating copy-paste artifacts, which is a real engineering contribution that is often under-reported in this space.

The core design choice — composing references into a single canvas with region-aware masking plus channel concatenation to inherit I2V capability — is well-motivated, and the ablation against token-wise concatenation and vanilla masking provides direct evidence for it.
Failure cases and limitations are honestly discussed (Appendix E.2, F.1), which increases credibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially an engineering combination of known ingredients — channel concatenation with temporal masks ([12]), layout/region-conditioned injection of text-attention values (cf. layout-guided diffusion, MS-Diffusion), and standard data augmentation. The paper frames these as three contributions, but each is incremental over prior work, and the positioning relative to SkyReels-A2 and Phantom could be sharper.

The subject disentanglement mechanism (Eq. 6) is technically under-specified: it is unclear which cross-attention layer(s) the 'value embeddings' are taken from, how a value vector v_i broadcasts against a spatial mask in the latent space, how the injection strength alpha is chosen, and why injecting into the first frame only suffices. No sensitivity analysis of alpha is provided.

Reproducibility is weak on key details: the dataset scale, number of training steps, GPU count/training cost, and the specifics of the 'state-of-the-art image generation model' used in Stage 4 are never disclosed; the GitHub and project page links in the paper are empty. Model scale and inference cost of MAGREF are also not reported.

Evaluation has fairness and robustness concerns: (i) 120 test cases is a small benchmark, partly self-curated, and the benchmark itself is a contribution from the authors evaluating their own method; (ii) compared commercial models run at different resolutions/frame rates (e.g., Vidu at 704x396), which can materially affect DINO/ArcFace-based similarity metrics; (iii) 'Total Score' is an unweighted average of heterogeneous metrics (aesthetic scores on a different scale than similarities), which is a questionable aggregation; (iv) no variance/statistical significance reporting.

Ablations are performed on a small-scale dataset with a large gap to the final model (0.587 vs. 0.627 Total Score), so component contributions at full scale are not directly verified; the cross-pair ablation drop (0.574 vs 0.580 for SD removal) is small and could be within noise.

Human ethics are insufficiently addressed: the method generates identity-preserving videos of real faces, and the data pipeline harvests faces from web video with only technical (not consent-based) filtering. There is no discussion of deepfake misuse, watermarking, or safeguards, which is a notable omission for this line of work.

Presentation quality is below the bar in places: duplicated references ([2]/[3], [16]/[17], [41]/[42]), typos ('mechansim'), missing baseline details in Figure 7 captions, and a vaguely described evaluation protocol for the user study (no details on how ties/prompts were controlled or statistical testing of win rates).
